hints: Look up the ionic radii of $\text{Na}^{+}$, $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$ in the Data Booklet and form the ratio $\text{cation radius} / \text{anion radius}$ for each chloride.
Match each calculated ratio to the range in the table to read off the geometry, then recall the co-ordination number that goes with octahedral and tetrahedral.
walkthrough:
Get the radius ratio idea clear**
Think of packing small cations into holes between larger anions. If the cation is very small it can only touch a few anions, if it is larger it can touch more. That is why the ratio $\text{cation radius} / \text{anion radius}$ tells you the geometry.

Calculate the two ratios**
From the Data Booklet $r(\text{Na}^{+}) = 0.095\text{ nm}$, $r(\text{Mg}^{2+}) = 0.065\text{ nm}$, $r(\text{Cl}^{-}) = 0.181\text{ nm}$. So: $$\frac{r(\text{Na}^{+})}{r(\text{Cl}^{-})} = \frac{0.095}{0.181} = 0.525$$ $$\frac{r(\text{Mg}^{2+})}{r(\text{Cl}^{-})} = \frac{0.065}{0.181} = 0.359$$

Read off geometry and co-ordination number**
$0.525$ lies in $0.414-0.732$, so $\text{Na}^{+}$ is octahedral. Octahedral means $6$ anions around each cation, so co-ordination number $= 6$. $0.359$ lies in $0.225-0.414$, so $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is tetrahedral. Tetrahedral means $4$ anions around each cation, so co-ordination number $= 4$.

Final answer: For $\text{NaCl}$: $0.095/0.181 = 0.525$, in range 0.414-0.732, so octahedral, co-ordination number of $\text{Na}^{+} = 6$.
For $\text{MgCl}_{2}$: $0.065/0.181 = 0.359$, in range 0.225-0.414, so tetrahedral, co-ordination number of $\text{Mg}^{2+} = 4$.

hints: Write $\Delta H_{r} = \Sigma \Delta H_{f}^{\ominus}(\text{products}) - \Sigma \Delta H_{f}^{\ominus}(\text{reactants})$, remembering to multiply $\Delta H_{f}^{\ominus}(\text{MgCl})$ by 2 and that $\Delta H_{f}^{\ominus}(\text{Mg(s)}) = 0$.
walkthrough:
Apply products minus reactants**
You are given formation enthalpies, so use Hess's law directly. For $$2\text{MgCl(s)} \rightarrow \text{Mg(s)} + \text{MgCl}_{2}\text{(s)}$$ $$\Delta H_{r} = [\Delta H_{f}^{\ominus}(\text{Mg}) + \Delta H_{f}^{\ominus}(\text{MgCl}_{2})] - [2 \times \Delta H_{f}^{\ominus}(\text{MgCl})]$$ $\text{Mg(s)}$ is an element in its standard state so its value is zero. Substitute: $$\Delta H_{r} = (-642) - (2 \times -106) = -642 + 212 = -430\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ The large negative value explains why $\text{MgCl}$ readily decomposes.

hints: Sketch the Born-Haber route for $\text{Mg(s)} + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{Cl}_{2}\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{MgCl(s)}$ via $\text{Mg(g)}$, $\text{Mg}^{+}\text{(g)} + \text{Cl(g)}$, then $\text{Mg}^{+}\text{(g)} + \text{Cl}^{-}\text{(g)}$.

Collect the needed terms: $\Delta H_{at}(\text{Mg}) = +147$, $\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta H_{at}(\text{Cl}_{2}) = +121$, $IE_{1}(\text{Mg}) = +736$ from the Data Booklet, $EA(\text{Cl}) = -349$, all in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.
Set $\Delta H_{f} = \Sigma$ of the cycle steps and rearrange to solve for lattice energy.
walkthrough:
Build the Born-Haber cycle in words**
Start from elements $\text{Mg(s)} + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{Cl}_{2}\text{(g)}$. Step 1: atomise Mg to $\text{Mg(g)}$, $+147\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. Step 2: atomise $\tfrac{1}{2}\text{Cl}_{2}$ to $\text{Cl(g)}$, $+121\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ (half of $+242$). Step 3: ionise $\text{Mg(g)} \rightarrow \text{Mg}^{+}\text{(g)} + e^{-}$, first ionisation energy $+736\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. Step 4: add electron $\text{Cl(g)} + e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Cl}^{-}\text{(g)}$, electron affinity $-349\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. Step 5: bring ions together $\text{Mg}^{+}\text{(g)} + \text{Cl}^{-}\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{MgCl(s)}$, lattice energy $\Delta H_{latt}$.

Equate the two routes**
Hess's law says direct formation equals sum of indirect steps: $$\Delta H_{f}^{\ominus}(\text{MgCl}) = \Delta H_{at}(\text{Mg}) + \tfrac{1}{2}\Delta H_{at}(\text{Cl}_{2}) + IE_{1}(\text{Mg}) + EA(\text{Cl}) + \Delta H_{latt}$$ $$-106 = 147 + 121 + 736 + (-349) + \Delta H_{latt}$$

Rearrange and evaluate**
$$\Delta H_{latt} = -106 -147 -121 -736 +349$$ $$\Delta H_{latt} = -761\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ Note this is for $\text{Mg}^{+}\text{(g)} + \text{Cl}^{-}\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{MgCl(s)}$, so only one $\text{Cl}$ and only first ionisation energy are used. That is the trap to avoid.

hints: Recall that lattice energy becomes more exothermic with higher ionic charge and smaller ionic radius, and compare the charges of $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ versus $\text{Mg}^{+}$ and $\text{Na}^{+}$.
For $\text{MgCl}_{2}$ versus $\text{MgCl}$, focus on why the $2+$ ion gives much stronger attraction than the $1+$ ion of the same element.
For $\text{NaCl}$ versus $\text{MgCl}$, both cations are $1+$, so focus on which $1+$ ion is smaller and packs closer to $\text{Cl}^{-}$.
walkthrough:
Recall what controls lattice energy**
Picture oppositely charged spheres pulling together. The pull is stronger when charge is higher and when distance between centres is shorter. So $\Delta H_{latt}$ is more negative for highly charged, small ions.

Compare $\text{MgCl}_{2}$ with $\text{MgCl}$**
$\text{MgCl}_{2}$ contains $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ while $\text{MgCl}$ contains $\text{Mg}^{+}$. The $2+$ ion has twice the charge and is also smaller because more protons pull on fewer electrons. Both factors greatly strengthen attraction to $\text{Cl}^{-}$, so lattice formation releases much more energy. Hence $\text{MgCl}_{2}$ is more exothermic.

Compare $\text{NaCl}$ with $\text{MgCl}$**
Here both cations are $1+$, $\text{Na}^{+}$ versus $\text{Mg}^{+}$. $\text{Mg}^{+}$ is larger (an extra shell effect and lower effective nuclear charge per electron than $\text{Na}^{+}$). $\text{Na}^{+}$ being smaller can approach $\text{Cl}^{-}$ more closely, so attraction is stronger and lattice energy is more negative for $\text{NaCl}$ than for $\text{MgCl}$.

Final answer: $\text{MgCl}_{2}$ lattice energy more exothermic / more negative than $\text{MgCl}$ because $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ has higher charge and smaller radius than $\text{Mg}^{+}$, giving stronger attraction.
$\text{NaCl}$ lattice energy more exothermic / more negative than $\text{MgCl}$ because $\text{Na}^{+}$ is smaller than $\text{Mg}^{+}$, giving stronger attraction.

hints: Start from the energy change when an electron is added to an atom or ion, and state the amount as per mole.
Remember Cambridge requires the exact state symbol for electron affinity, think about which state all species must be in.
walkthrough:
State the molar process**
Electron affinity is the energy change when $1$ mole of atoms or ions each gains an electron, equivalently $1$ mole of electrons is gained. For example: $$\text{Cl(g)} + e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Cl}^{-}\text{(g)}$$

Insist on gaseous**
The definition only works if everything is isolated gas particles with no lattice or solution effects. So you must say gaseous atoms and gaseous ions. Missing the word gaseous loses the mark.

Final answer: Energy change when one mole of gaseous atoms / ions gains one mole of electrons (to form one mole of gaseous 1- ions).
All species are gaseous.
